# Abstract

Michael Kerr presents a webinar exploring the convergence between systems biology and Bowen family systems theory, arguing that biological sciences are moving toward frameworks long familiar to Bowen theorists. Drawing on recent cancer research literature, particularly work by Marta Bertoluzzo and colleagues on niche reconstruction, Kerr examines how cancer arises not from driver genes alone but from breakdown of healthy tissue niches into cancer-permissive environments. He introduces the extended evolutionary synthesis, which emphasizes developmental processes and relational biology over genetic reductionism, and discusses how cancer can be understood as morphogenesis gone awry. Kerr then explores the role of the autonomic nervous system and neuroendocrine signaling in tumor progression, connecting chronic stress and allostatic load to cancer outcomes. He draws explicit parallels between the figure-ground shift in cancer treatment—moving from targeting cancer cells to reconstructing niches—and the Bowenian clinical move of shifting focus from the identified patient to the family system. The presentation demonstrates that systems biology increasingly recognizes the importance of understanding dynamic relationships between cellular, organismic, and environmental factors, a perspective central to Bowen theory's approach to human functioning.
